They just play ratatoude. Funky butt, funky butt, take it away. I heard that head wouldn't. Come on, Chef. Did I send you all, girl?
Tunes that they played. Uh-huh. What were some of the other tunes like that they played by head?
All different tunes. Funky butt, take it away. Wonder why my baby gone tonight. All different tunes, you know? Made up, made up. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Who was the best...
Who was the best person to make up tunes? Was it some band that... Played drums, played trumpet? No, that could make up tunes like that.
Oh, you, like you and the band, you make one and I'll make one. I'd sing a song and we'd play it and then we'd... The whole band would play it.
Practice it through. Mm-hmm. Well, who was the best at that? What? Who had the best make up tunes?
Um, well, this brother just called his name... Charlie Klim. He was a king.
He could make up good tunes?
Oh, man. He could take anything and make a rag out of it.
Was he related to Edward Klim? That's right. That's right.
You know him. This is Charlie Klim? Yeah, Charlie Klim and Edward Klim. Two brothers. Oh, they were brothers.
And where did Charlie play?
Hold on, played trumpet. Oh, I see.

Was Charlie older? Uh-huh. Was Charlie older? Yeah. Charlie... Edward was older. Mm-hmm. Did you know Happy Galloway? Huh? I think it was Charlie Galloway. Oh, Galloway. I wasn't talking Galloway. I don't know if he was a person. Did you know an accordion player named Peyton? Huh? Did you know an accordion player named Peyton?
Oh, Big Fat Peyton, yeah. Sure do, man. I was a kid. He used to play in Franklin Street.

What would he play? Who? Oh, he had different numbers, yeah. All of them played different shoes. Oh, he had different numbers. All of them played different shoes. All of them played different shoes. All of them played different shoes.
All of them played different shoes. How did they play different shoes?
How did they play different shoes? How did they play different shoes?
How did they play different shoes? played different shows. All of them played different, you know. Every band had a favorite, you understand?
Yeah. What were some of the favorites bands had? Uh-huh. What were some of the favorites bands had? Oh, different things, I can't remember. No.

Every band had a different, different tune. Two in there would play different. Did you have one for your band? My band? Yeah, we played different tune. Funky boy, take it away. Wonder where my baby's gone tonight. All such things, we named them ourselves, you know. Did you sing a little bit of I Wonder Where My Baby's Gone Tonight? Uh-huh.
Do you remember the words to that? Oh, yeah. Did you sing it?
You saw it, no. Oh.
What were the words like on I Wonder Where My Baby's Gone Tonight? What were the words to I Wonder Where My Baby's Gone Tonight? That's it, what you say now. And that's all?

Different things, people and the harmony come in, you know. Oh, yeah. Down in the trial part you play the trial of your own, you know what you mean? Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Now, what was the second band you played with? Do you remember that very well? The second band?
Yes. The first band, yeah, the Lions Band, oh yeah. The Lions Band. Lions, right across the street there. Mm-hmm. I was the manager of the Lions Band, right across the street there. Mm-hmm.
I was the manager of the Lions Band, right across the street there. Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Oh, yes.
You see, I got a job out of the management of the band. I was in the Hop Goblins band. They had a band called the Hop Goblins. On Halloween night, it was a big night for the Goblins, you know?
Yes.

So, I get a job, $90, for liberty. And he arrived right now. He wasn't born then. He lived. Wasn't thought of. And I get this job and I pick out 11 men beside myself. 12 men to play that $90 job, you know? We had 35 men in the Garbage van, you know? So, the fellas I didn't pick out, they got committed, Captain Jones, and brought them to my house on a Friday. We went down there on the Central Rock Street. So, Captain Jones called me and said, well, Paola, I'll tell you all that job left for the first. I said, yes, it is. He said, well, did you take that job on the Goblins man? I said, I did. He said, well, I'll tell you, Paola. If you take that job on, on and back and then, every man in the Goblins man got to play that job. I said, you're right, Captain. Captain Jones is in here on time. That's, that's on a Friday. I said, he's right, too. I said, but you fellas, what I'll pick out, remember what I'll tell you. I said, white pants, blue blouse, white collar, black tie, white cap. And meet me, grab you in Saratoga for eight o'clock morning, morning. I comes on up to town, boy, I didn't work that day. I drive, drive the float then. I went up and I met the fella, I had the job changed. I go to the honor. By the past, there was all the Goblins man there, and I got this pretty blue suit. Yeah, I come. But my nephew, back there, was the first bass drummer. He wouldn't, he didn't want to play. And that made me have to take it, you know. So I took the beat of Saratoga. Went on to replace that job. He goes up to the Tulane Club, you know I did. I was there the other day. Yeah, I was. Went up there to meet him. Said, well, everybody in the Uricka band, I named the band myself Uricka. Picked that name out of the man Ricka. Everybody in the Uricka band is excuse for me, put all the, all the Uricka bands out. You understand? And that band been going by Uricka ever since. That's the only standard band, brass band they got here. Uricka. My daughter, my oldest granddaughter, she's the godmother that band, she's Christmas. Made right up in my house. You know, it's in college.
What year was that about? Oh, I just remember now. Was it after World War I or before?
Oh, before World War I, man. Well, before that.
Was it before the big storm?
Right that year, yeah, that year was the big storm. Yeah, that year was big storm. I made that band up myself. I just, and named it the Uricka band.
And who was in it then?
Oh, Lord, I couldn't call all them fellas names. I was in it. Willie Wilson, Johnny Wilson, Shepard.
What did the Wilsons play? Huh? What instruments did they play?
Willie Wilson was the leader. Mm-hmm. Johnny Wilson and Barrett don't play. Mm-hmm.
Shepard you said? Uh-huh. There was a fellow named Shepard? Shepard? Shepard?
What was it?
Oh.

Shepard was a trombone player. Molly was a trombone player. Buddy Alphonse played alto. Who else? Who else? Who else played alto? I didn't know where she had. Did you have a clarinet? At that time, no, sir. Didn't have no clarinet. You know what I'm talking about?
No. We didn't have no clarinet in the, in the, in the, what you call it, but we had a clarinet in the tundra band.

Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. But I was playing clarinet in the tundra. Who was playing a sousaphona tuba with that, you read the clarinet? Who was playing a clarinet in the tundra? Who was playing a clarinet in the tundra? Who was playing a clarinet in the tundra? Mm-hmm. Who was playing a clarinet in the tundra? No, we didn't have the clowning in the, in the, what you call, we had the clowning in the turner. But I was playing clowning in the turner.
Who was playing a sousaphone or tuba with that eureka? My brother.
Yeah, my brother was a boot band.
And it was a snare drummer?
A snare drummer at that time? Mm-hmm. All he got is two legs cut off now.
Oh. Arthur Obey. I know him. He lives back in town. Yeah, he lives right back in John Brunius' house. I saw him Saturday and Sunday, I saw him on this.
Well, that's one of the best street drums we had. Obey, we called him, Obey.
And who was playing bass drum? Me.
I played bass drum in the, in the, um, Eureka. And I played clowning at the turner.
I see.
And at that. But Art Ogen was a snare drummer to Eureka.
Mm-hmm. Did you have a, how many trumpets? Well, I don't know when I had three.
Willie Wilson, you say?
Willie Wilson. Willie Wilson.

Willie Wilson. Willie Wilson and Zeo. I call it Zeno. Yeah, Zeno played trumpet. And what other player played trumpet? Willie Webber. Willie Wilson. Willie Wilson. Willie Wilson. Oh, I see. Good. Willie Wilson. And Tom Albert played? Huh? Tom Albert. Tom Albert. And Tom Albert played?
Huh? Tom Albert. And Tom Albert played? Huh? Tom Albert. Yeah. When, when was he with you? Huh? When was Tom Albert with you?
Oh, he, he, he just quit the band here and got too old to play. Oh, I see. He don't play no more.
When was he with you? When was Tom Albuquerque with you?
Oh he just quit the band here and got too old to play. He don't play no more. Yes I know. Oh he first was a violin player. To play violin. He live out there on McGonagall

Street somewhere. Oh yeah we know. Was he with the Eureka when you first started that? Uh huh. Was he with the Eureka when you started the band? When I was with me. No he wasn't. He came brought by later? He was playing the violin and he quit playing the violin with me on the trumpet.
Whose place did he take? He's a good trumpet player. He's a member of the Eureka brass band but he don't play no more.
Whose place did he take? Huh? Whose place did he take? Who? Whose place did he take in the band?

Whose place? Yes. Oh he take my... Whose place did he take? Let's see what place did he have. Whose place did he take? What place did he take? What place did he take? New Rodriguez I've been here. Yeah he took me to the band. That's where the Eureka? That's Eureka yeah.
Well how did the Eureka get his name? How did you ever get that name for it?

I don't know I'm the one giving it. Yes. I listen. They had some... I used to bum in a yard down there. And they had some watched indie boys you know? Yes. And they all, they were musicians. But they didn't let, I didn't let them know I could play you know? So I used to, they used to make a drink every, every, they'd get paid every Tuesday. And they'd come in and smoke. They'd make a nice drink with it. So on Saturday I said well Saturday my payday I won't make a drink. Buy the stuff too. No, of course they treated Tuesday. I go on down and I buy. Then they begin to talk about their band at home, Eureka. And I kept that in mind. And when I was signed that contract I signed it Eureka. All they got, they got fellas in the Eureka. Babe, didn't know how it come to be named Eureka. Yes. Sonny Henry, he must know cause he was in the Eureka. Years ago.
How old is Sonny Henry now? Oh I don't know. I got to be. Me and Sonny come up together.
He's about your age then huh? Yeah, no I don't think he's old as I am. Might be, I don't know.
Did you know Willie Connish? Willie Connish? Sure.
Who did he play with? Who, Connish? Yes. Oh he played in a tipping band.

I had a band called the Eagle Brass Band uptown. Well he was trumpet, uh, strong and played with. Old big carnage. Was he playing Eureka too? Yeah. He, uh, this boy, this great trumpet player from the other corner, Lewis, Lewis what? What do you call it? Armstrong. Armstrong. Lewis and him lying together. And, you know, every time Armstrong meet, me, Darcony, he says, you're yet spitting in that trombone, you're yet to be kidding him, you know? He dead now, you know?

I saw his wife, uh, Friday. You did? She lives right around the corner from the Tulane Club. Yeah. I gotta go back and see her sometime. She seemed like a very nice lady. Yes, ma'am. I was getting in the car with a trombone player, Clement Tervalon, and she said, my husband used to play that instrument. Yeah. Willie Connish's wife. Willie Connish's wife. Just, just by being with a trombone player, I found her. Oh, uh. I was with, uh, this fella, Clement Tervalon. He works with Clement Tervalon. He's Burbank's nephew. He works with, uh, John Casimir on the street.

Oh, on the street back. Yeah. Did you know Frankie Dooson? Oh, yes, sir, man. Well, he was a wonderful, uh, uh, what's it called, uh, rotina. Mm-hmm. He was a rotina Frankie Dooson. Tall, brown, silver. Well, where was he from?
All right, right across the room. Mm-hmm. Um, a motor room. And who did he work with?
Well, everybody. Anybody. Mm-hmm. Didn't have no particular band. Oh, did they have an Eagle Dance Band? That's the band. That's the band. The Eagle Brass Band.

Well, they had a dance band, or no? Brass band. Eagle Brass. Oh, they had a brass band. Eagle Brass Band. And Cornish was in there. Who? You say Cornish was in there. Cornish was a trombone player, yeah. Mm-hmm. Did he play slide or valve trombone?

He played, uh, valve first. Then they all went to getting slides, you know. Mm-hmm. Do you ever bunk Johnson? Sure, man. You had no bunk. Been no bunk for him. Before he died. Oh, he was a good little
trumpet player. What kind of fellow was he?
Nice fellow. Generalified, you know. I don't know about him reading or what, but I know he was a good head worker.
Who was the best head musician, ragtime musician, when you came out?
That boy, Clem, I'll tell you about. Clem? Yeah. Best routine man. And, uh, Bolden. They were the best. Them was the best ragtime in there. Edward or Charlie Clem? Charlie Clem.
Yeah. And, uh, who was the best of all the reading musicians?
Uh, who was the best? For reading. Oh, Manuel Perez.
Manuel Perez. Yes, indeed. Well, would he play with the same tone as Bolden and Clem?
No, no, he had his own band.
But that, I said, would he have the same tone?
Oh, sure, yeah. He was a, he was a trumpet player.
Would their style be alike? Huh? Would they sound alike? Would their style be alike? Uh, Bolden and, uh, Perez? What would be the difference in the way they played?
Yeah, they'd be different.
They'd be different, huh?

Yeah, but that, that, that man of Perez, you see the book wouldn't tell you about it. You have, you see the red book? Yes, I have. Yeah, alright. You see down there. Whatever, not a trumpet player you got. Uh, huh.
Now, uh, remember tape chambers? Sure. What kind of fellow was he? He was a nice boy. He was a nice fellow. Played good music?
Yeah, he could breathe. Sure, I know. No, I know. Roy Palmer?
Who? Roy Palmer? Yeah, Roy.
Where do you play trombone? Uh, huh.
He's living in Chicago now. Yeah. He's living in Chicago now.
Did he, did he read too? Huh?
Did Roy read? Yeah, he read too. Yeah. He read too.

Yeah. You know, I've had many piano players around town. Piano players? Who? Piano? Piano. Well, the best piano player I've ever heard of. I've never known. We live out there by Albert, Tom Albert now. Right fellow. Mm-hm. Right fellow. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Walter Deco? Walter Deco? Walter Deco?

Do you know Walter Deco? That's who I'm talking about. Yeah, he's a great fellow. Oh, yeah. Well, the best piano player I've ever heard of. I've never known him. We live out there by Albert, Tom Albert now.
Mm-hm.
Right fellow.
Oh, yeah. Walter Deco? Mm-hm. Walter Deco? Mm-hm. Walter Deco? Do you know Walter Deco? Mm-hm.
Walter Deco? Do you know Walter Deco?

That's who I'm talking about. Yeah. He killed the fellow. He killed the, uh, they come play. Gaier, he killed Gaier. Mm-hm. Walter Deco, he had that by Albert. He killed by Albert. He killed by Albert.
Now what, did he play in a band or did he play? Oh, yeah, man.

He had his own band. They used to play at the Dog House. Mm-hm. That was their job. That's why he killed Gaier. Stab Gaier up there. Gaier was, uh, Gaier was, uh, Gaier was, uh, a vet up there. Who's an animal? Hi.
Hi. Hi. You remember Ann Cook? Ann Cook? I reckon I do. Old Ann Cook. Is she living? Yes, she is.
Ann Cook. I saw a few monkey dogs. She's blind now. She's not there yet? Still on thing. Thank you, Mr. Perry. Did she sing much? Huh?
Did she do much singing? Did she sing? Uh-huh. Did you hear her sing? I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know what they're not coming.
But I know from the country.
She come from down below the barrack. Where they call Praet Hatfield. Oh, yes. That's why she comes.
How old is she? She dear age? She dear age like that. How old is she? How old is she? How old is she? How old is she? How old is she? How old is she?
How old is she? How old is she? How old is she? She was raised around that time.
How old is she? Do you know?
Oh, I know. Oh, I know. She used to be a hustler in the district, you know?
Yes. Did they have many singers?
Huh?
Did they have many singers when you were coming out? Songsters? Yeah, songsters.
No, a few of them. I never worried about them.
Well, did they work with bands?
Yeah, they had women used to sing with the band, you know?
Oh, yeah.
And women used to sing with the band. Did you know Mamie Desdum? Mm-hmm.
Mamie Desdum? Did you know her? Who? Mamie Desdum.
She said, yeah.
You knew maybe Desdunes you said? You knew maybe Desdunes? Desdunes, I heard of Desdunes. Actually, they lived on Culledama Street. Yeah, okay. Yeah, I heard of Desdunes.

segments.title: Manuel Perez and opening chatter
segments.summary: Interviewer checks the recording level and asks about Manuel Perez, whom Parker calls a wonderful trumpet player.

segments.title: Meeting Albert Glenn and Hope's Hall
segments.summary: Parker recalls Albert Glenn rooming with his father when Parker was a boy, and being taken to a dance hall.

segments.title: Dauphin's accordion band and its players
segments.summary: Parker names accordionist Dauphin as leader of the seven-piece band with Albert Glenn on bass, the Santiagos, and Bad Frank.

segments.title: Birth and being raised by his godmother
segments.summary: Born 4 March 1875, Parker was given to his godmother and did not see his mother until 19; he tells of following his sister home.

segments.title: Life in the city, brother Joe and the riverfront strike
segments.summary: Parker came to the city young, got long pants from his brother Joe, named siblings, and recalled a strike killing.

segments.title: Musical family and buying an alto horn
segments.summary: Parker's father, brother and brother-in-law were musicians; he tells of seeing an alto sax at a shop, and where they lived.

segments.title: Ben Coe's band and its members
segments.summary: Parker names the oldest musicians he heard, Ben Coe's band and its members, with talk of Jim Robinson's relatives and a church parade.

segments.chapter: First bands and brass band practice
segments.title: Parker's first band, the Terminal Band, and its lineup
segments.summary: Parker made up his first band; he and the interviewer list the members and instruments, including Bracey, Piazza, Sheikode and brother Joe.

segments.chapter: First bands and brass band practice
segments.title: Reading music and the country brass band teacher
segments.summary: Parker's band read music taught by professors; Jim Humphrey taught country bands in the parishes.

segments.chapter: First bands and brass band practice
segments.title: Brass band repertoire: marches, funeral music and hymns
segments.summary: Parker says brass bands played marches, funeral dirges and hymns, some from music and some by head.

segments.chapter: First bands and brass band practice
segments.title: Church excursions and dances played by brass bands
segments.summary: Parker lost a job playing Monday church excursions; talk of dances, polkas, brass bands at fairgrounds, and string bands in the district.

segments.chapter: First bands and brass band practice
segments.title: Blues and string bands in the district
segments.summary: Brief talk about the district's string bands and the blues being sung first.

segments.title: Edward Clem and Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: Parker recalls trumpeter Edward Clem and Buddy Bolden as blues king, reading and playing at Dixie Park.

segments.title: Playing by head and ragtime tunes
segments.summary: Parker discusses bands playing by head, ragtime, made-up tunes like Funky Butt, and who made up tunes best.

segments.title: Charlie Clem and accordionist Peyton
segments.summary: Charlie Clem could make a rag out of anything; he and Edward were brothers; Big Fat Peyton played on Franklin Street.

segments.title: The Hop Goblins job and forming his own band
segments.summary: Parker tells of managing the Lions Band, a Halloween job for the Goblins, and making up a band the year of the big storm.

segments.title: Eureka Brass Band members and instruments
segments.summary: Parker lists the Eureka lineup including Willie Wilson, Zeno, Art Ogle and Tom Albert, and who played what.

segments.title: How the Eureka got its name
segments.summary: Parker explains he heard the name Eureka from men he worked with in a yard and used it for his band.

segments.chapter: Players and singers of the era
segments.title: Willie Cornish, Eagle Brass Band and Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: Talk of trombonist Willie Cornish and the Eagle Brass Band, Frankie Dusen, and Bunk Johnson as a good head worker.

segments.chapter: Players and singers of the era
segments.title: Best ragtime and reading trumpeters: Clem, Bolden, Perez
segments.summary: Parker ranks Charlie Clem and Bolden best at ragtime and Manuel Perez best reader; their styles differ.

segments.chapter: Players and singers of the era
segments.title: Other players: Roy Palmer and pianist Walter Decou
segments.summary: Brief comments on Tape Chambers, Roy Palmer and the pianist Walter Decou and his killing of Gaier.

segments.chapter: Players and singers of the era
segments.title: Ann Cook and women singers with bands
segments.summary: Parker recalls Ann Cook, a district hustler, and says women sang with bands; Mamie Desdunes is raised.
